description:
Our team brings together a diverse range of skills, including Machine Learning, Web Development, Programming,  and Critical Thinking. We believe in collaboration, creative problem-solving and combining our technical strengths to transform ideas into meaningful impact.

we are exploring how NASA Earth observation data and emerging technologies can support smarter crop rotation decisions, improve soil health and help farmers adapt to changing climate and environmental conditions.
summary:
AGRONEX is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make informed, climate-aware and economically sound farming decisions using NASA Earth observation data and agricultural information.

The platform combines satellite-derived environmental insights, such as rainfall, temperature, vegetation and soil moisture indicators, with local agricultural knowledge. It enables farmers to compare crop rotation strategies, assess potential risks and trade-offs, and understand the uncertainty surrounding available data.

Beyond environmental analysis, AGRONEX provides location-based crop market prices and estimates the cost of starting cultivation, expected production expenses, potential revenue and estimated profit. This helps farmers evaluate both the agricultural suitability and financial viability of different crops before investing.

AGRONEX addresses the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge by transforming Earth observation data into practical farming insights. It is important because it helps farmers make better-informed decisions, adapt to changing environmental conditions, manage financial risks and work towards more sustainable and profitable farming.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Every farming season starts with the same two questions: what do I plant, and when? Agronex answers them from a phone. The farmer finds their farm by GPS or by typing their town, and can pin the field on a satellite map. Agronex then reads NASA’s climate record (NASA POWER) to find when the rainy seasons start and end, including mid-season dry spells, and scores how well each crop’s needs fit that weather. After five simple questions about your farm, such as what grew there before, it builds rotation plans, such as maize followed by cowpea, that check legume cycles and crop families. Alongside the plan, the farmer sees a seven-day forecast, NASA satellite soil moisture (SMAP, quality-filtered) and the previous day’s rainfall (GPM IMERG, only for complete days) through Google Earth Engine, and recorded Ghana MoFA market prices. The main screens work in English, Asante Twi and Ewe, and can be read aloud.

What benefits does it have?

The benefits are to everybody. They reach the farmer, who can plant crops knowing he won’t be weathered down by the climate, and they reach us, the people who will have more food in our markets because of good crop yields from better soil health. The farmer also gets a rotation that rebuilds the soil while still earning money, and can test an income scenario with their own yield and costs before spending on seed. A farmer who can’t read English well gets the same quality of advice as anyone else, because Agronex speaks and shows it, not only writes it.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The impact is to have farmers be able to grow crops no matter the climate or weather, by having the information to make better decisions. Only about 3% of Ghana’s cultivated land is irrigated (World Bank, via B&FT Online), so most farmers live on the rain, and the same NASA data covers rain-fed farming across Sub-Saharan Africa and beyond. We aim for more farmers using soil-friendly rotations, less soil lost to erosion, more varied household food and better margins from choosing crops with evidence. These are goals we are working toward, not results we have measured yet.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We used a lot of APIs, Twi and Ewe translations, Python and React, and the GOAT, VS Code. The backend is Python with FastAPI, using SQLite for local data. The frontend is a mobile-first React and TypeScript web app, built with Vite and Tailwind CSS, with charts and a Progressive Web App setup. For data we used NASA POWER, NASA SMAP and NASA GPM IMERG through Google Earth Engine, Open-Meteo for forecasts, Leaflet with satellite map tiles for the field map, and Ghana MoFA market prices. Khaya provides the Twi and Ewe speech.

How is your project creative?

Inasmuch as humans love to control things, our project was a kind of go with the flow, and you still get a good way ahead. Someone might be stubborn and still grow whatever they want even when the climate cannot support it, but life is about rolling with the punches and learning something. In this case it is crop rotation, a beautiful way to keep our soils healthy while making a good amount of money. Agronex doesn’t forbid anyone from growing what they want. It shows how well the weather fits, what a rotation could do and what the market recorded, and the farmer decides. It’s also honest about its data: every reading names its source, and when a satellite reading or a price isn’t available, the app says so, and anything shown for demonstration is labelled as demo. Five questions, one plan, in your own language, read aloud if you like. Elegant in its simplicity.

What factors did your team consider?

The educational level of the everyday farmer in Ghana, for one: many farmers have limited formal schooling and are not comfortable reading English, so we built for the ear and the eye, with Twi, Ewe, read-aloud, big buttons and a high-contrast mode. Market prices were another, because a crop that grows well but can’t sell helps no one, so plans sit next to recorded prices and an income scenario the farmer fills in themselves. We were also careful with the science: SMAP reads about 9 km cells, so we never present it as a sensor in the field or tell anyone to irrigate, and long-cycle crops like cocoa are not forced into a single rainy season. Finally, access and privacy: data is expensive and signal is patchy, so the language packs are bundled in the app, and once it has loaded, switching language works without a connection. There is also no sign-up, no password and no personal account.
